text: LaLonde (1986) set aside the NSW experimental controls, used CPS and PSID comparison groups, and found that many nonexperimental estimators did not replicate the experimental impact on 1978 earnings ($886 for NSW men in his sample, Table 5).

The CPS comparison group is the March 1976 CPS matched to Social Security earnings, restricted to people in the labor force with nominal income below $20,000 and household income below $30,000; in 1976, 21 percent of the males had earnings at the Social Security maximum (LaLonde 1986, footnote, pp. 611-612).

Dehejia and Wahba (1999) restrict LaLonde's NSW men to the subsample with 1974 earnings, defined by month of assignment, giving 185 treated and 260 control men; the CPS-1 comparison group has 15,992 men.

The experimental benchmark for the Dehejia-Wahba subsample is $1,794 (standard error 633) in 1982 dollars, the difference in mean 1978 earnings between treated and experimental control men (Dehejia and Wahba 1999, Tables 2-3).

Using CPS-1, Dehejia and Wahba (1999, Table 3) obtain propensity-score stratification estimates of $1,713 (unadjusted) and $1,774 (adjusted) and matching estimates of $1,582 and $1,616, against -$8,498 for the raw difference in means.
Dehejia and Wahba choose their propensity-score specification by adding higher-order and interaction terms until covariates balance within strata.

Smith and Todd (2005) find that low-bias propensity-score matching estimates are highly sensitive to the Dehejia-Wahba choice of subsample and to the variables in the score, and that difference-in-differences matching performs best, which they attribute to geographic mismatch and to earnings measured differently for participants and comparison units.

Dehejia (2005) replies that a separate propensity-score specification is needed for each treatment-comparison combination and that sensitivity to small specification changes is a diagnostic of comparison-group quality.

Imbens (2015) proposes trimming and assessing unconfoundedness with pseudo-outcomes without using outcome data, followed by an analysis stage with no specification search; on the nonexperimental Lalonde data his matched-sample estimates range from $1,720 to $2,100, but pseudo-outcome tests reject the null of no effect on 1975 earnings.

Imbens and Xu (2025) find that on the LaLonde-Dehejia-Wahba CPS sample all ten modern estimators they apply yield positive ATT estimates, several close to the $1,794 benchmark, and that estimates become more similar after trimming for overlap.

Imbens and Xu (2025) find that placebo estimates with 1975 earnings as the outcome are large, negative and statistically significant for all nonexperimental estimators, so the placebo test does not support unconfoundedness in the LaLonde data.
When treated units lacking comparable controls are trimmed, the experimental benchmark for the remaining 164 treated men in the Imbens-Xu trimmed LDW-CPS sample is $1,911 rather than $1,794.
Advani, Kitagawa and Słoczyński (2019) find that empirical Monte Carlo procedures applied to the NSW-CPS data are worse than random at selecting the estimator with the smallest absolute bias.
Athey et al. (2024) find, in simulations calibrated to the LaLonde-Dehejia-Wahba data, that no single average-treatment-effect estimator outperforms the others in all settings.
Abadie and Imbens (2011) propose a bias-corrected nearest-neighbour matching estimator and apply it to the NSW data originally analysed by LaLonde (1986).
Crump et al. (2009) show that a good approximation to the optimal subsample under limited overlap drops units with estimated propensity scores outside [0.1, 0.9].
Rubin (2008) argues that observational studies should be designed to approximate randomized experiments without examining any outcome data.

The NSW Dehejia-Wahba subsample and the CPS comparison group are distributed by Rajeev Dehejia, with the column order treatment, age, education, black, hispanic, married, nodegree, RE74, RE75, RE78; the page states no explicit licence.

Cook, Shadish and Wong (2008) list among the criteria for a within-study comparison that analysts of the experimental and observational data be blind to each other's results, and that the experiment and observational study estimate the same causal quantity with groups measured in the same way.

Within-study comparisons with pre-specified or preregistered observational analyses exist outside the NSW benchmark: Weidmann and Miratrix (2021) specified their matching method before generating results, and Keller et al. (2024) preregistered the analysis plan of a four-arm within-study comparison.
